prize_parts.citation: for the design of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that enable delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: Ionizable lipid nanoparticles are molecular design and self-assembly put to work: pKa-tuned lipids that are near neutral in blood and charged in the endosome, packing behaviour that drives encapsulation and membrane fusion, and scalable controlled mixing. This solved the delivery problem that kept siRNA and mRNA from being medicines, and it changed what clinicians can actually do (patisiran, the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, and now in vivo gene-editing payloads). The work is decades old, independently reproduced, clinically validated at global scale, and four of the eight openings (mine, Sparr, Chabes, Aqvist) already place it in their top five, which suggests it is not only my taste for translational chemistry. It is also a chemistry-framed complement to the 2023 Medicine prize: that prize rewarded what is delivered, this one would reward the vehicle.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Credit is spread across the Vancouver encapsulation and ionizable-lipid line (Cullis, Madden, Hope, MacLachlan) and the combinatorial lipidoid line (Anderson, Langer), and a three-person limit forces a contestable choice that no opening ballot agrees on exactly. A second worry is whether the committee sees it as pharmaceutical formulation rather than fundamental chemistry, and whether the 2023 Medicine prize makes some members feel the area has already been honoured. I have not verified patent and priority details.

responses.point: Sparr ranks B019 first as lipid self-assembly and phase behaviour (pH-dependent charge, inverted-phase propensity, controlled particle formation) and proposes Cullis, Madden and Hope, attributing the decisive formulation work to the Vancouver group.
responses.response: I agree with the physical-chemistry framing and it strengthens the case that this is chemistry and not merely formulation. Where I differ is on attribution. Leaving out Anderson means leaving out the lipid-design and screening line that produced the high-potency ionizable lipids used in the approved siRNA product and later mRNA work, so I keep Anderson alongside Cullis and Madden. I would still like us to test whether the committee thinks the decisive step was the Vancouver encapsulation chemistry or the lipid screening, since that decides between your trio and mine.

responses.point: Chabes ranks B056 first because induced proximity and the cereblon discovery give a general, catalytic way to remove any protein and explain thalidomide at the molecular level, and he places B019 third.
responses.response: I take the cereblon argument seriously; it is why I rank B056 second. My hesitation is maturity: no PROTAC degrader is approved, so the concept still lacks the clinical vindication that LNPs have. I would not call B056 premature, but I would put the molecular-glue and cereblon line ahead of PROTAC as the more settled part, and I would worry that three names cannot cover Crews, Deshaies, Handa, Ciulli and Gray fairly. If the committee wants a degradation prize I would rather see it follow one more round of clinical evidence than compete with B019 now.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks Car and Parrinello (B058) first as an original, clean, quantitatively tested theory whose consequences are field-wide, with only two names and little credit dispute, and ranks B019 fifth.
responses.response: The Car-Parrinello attribution is cleaner than anything I can offer for B019, and I do not dispute the standard. But clean credit and four decades of use do not by themselves answer which discovery deserves the prize this year. B019 also has a physical and quantitative mechanism, and in addition it shows the downstream test I weigh most: the chemistry enabled a new class of medicines. I am not arguing B058 is unworthy, only that it can wait without a loss, and that B019 has the stronger case on consequence.

responses.point: Linke ranks nanopore sequencing (B017) first as a clean physical principle, ionic-current blockade as a readout of chemical identity, that became a widely deployed long-read technology, and proposes Deamer, Akeson and Bayley.
responses.response: I ranked B017 third and agree it is mature and a real analytical capability. My qualification is that the attribution depends on separating the 1996 translocation demonstration from engineered pores and enzyme-ratcheted reading, and that Branton's status (I recall he has died but have not confirmed) could change the configuration. I also think it is more naturally read as measurement physics and biotechnology than as molecular design, which is the reason I put it behind the lipid case. If the committee prefers analytical chemistry, I would support it as an alternative or as the second part of a two-part prize.

uncertainties: Which Vancouver and lipidoid contributors have the strongest claim, and whether Hope, MacLachlan or Langer should displace Madden or Anderson in a three-person set.
Whether the committee regards LNP delivery as fundamental chemistry or pharmaceutical formulation, and whether the 2023 Medicine prize reduces appetite for it.
Whether clinical evidence for PROTACs and molecular glues will mature enough to make B056 the stronger option in a future year.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My postdoc mentors (Molly Stevens, Freddy Boey) and my Linkoping biosensor and peptide work have no direct link to the shortlisted candidates, though my interest in nanoparticle-based biomedicine and my fellow new member Emma Sparr's overlap in self-assembly are shared perspectives, not a recusal issue.
